title: Trump Signs Nuclear Deal With Saudi Arabia, Sparking Proliferation Fears Across the Middle East
excerpt: The 30-year agreement could allow Riyadh to enrich uranium without the strictest international safeguards, drawing sharp criticism from arms control experts and some lawmakers.
body:
• The Trump administration signed a 30-year nuclear cooperation agreement (123 Agreement) with Saudi Arabia that could allow the kingdom to enrich uranium for civilian reactors.
  • The deal does not include the "Gold Standard" safeguards that would block enrichment and reprocessing — both potential pathways to nuclear weapons — nor the IAEA's Additional Protocol for snap inspections.
  • Trump said the deal is contingent on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalising relations with Israel, a condition Riyadh has not publicly accepted.
  • Arms control experts warn the agreement could set a global precedent for weakened nuclear safeguards and ignite a regional arms race.

What the Deal Contains

President Donald Trump approved a landmark nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia last week, clearing the way for American companies to provide technology and expertise for a Saudi civilian nuclear programme. The Department of Energy announced the deal's signature on Wednesday, sending it to Congress for a mandatory review period.

The agreement, known as a Section 123 Agreement under the U.S. Atomic Energy Act, would last 30 years. It would allow a joint U.S.-Saudi team to explore whether uranium enrichment is warranted and commercially viable. If enrichment proceeds, Americans would build the facility without transferring the sensitive technology to Riyadh.

The deal bars Saudi Arabia from independently developing enrichment technology or purchasing it from other countries for a decade, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Missing Safeguards

What the deal does not include has drawn the sharpest criticism. It lacks the "Gold Standard" — safeguards the U.S. has long insisted on in nuclear agreements that would block enrichment and reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel, both potential pathways to weapons. It also does not require Saudi Arabia to sign the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, which grants inspectors the power to carry out snap inspections at undeclared locations.

"The agreement itself was reckless and irresponsible, but the broader ramifications could be felt for years to come."

— Kelsey Davenport, Director for Nonproliferation Policy, Arms Control Association

Energy Secretary Chris Wright defended the deal, arguing it "upholds the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation." Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed concerns, telling reporters that the U.S. would not "reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation."

The Abraham Accords Condition

Trump tied the deal to a broader diplomatic ambition. In a social media post, he said the agreement "will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords." The Saudi Embassy in Washington declined to comment on the condition.

The Saudis have made clear that normalising relations with Israel would require a clear path for Palestinian statehood — a condition Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected as untenable for Israel's security.

Regional Implications

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that if Iran ever develops a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would follow suit. Critics fear the deal, even if intended for civilian power, could eventually bring the kingdom to the threshold of weapons capability — and force regional powers like Egypt and Turkey to pursue their own programmes.

The deal's supporters counter that without U.S. involvement, competitors like China and Russia would step in, giving Washington less influence over the Saudi programme.

For India, which has its own nuclear cooperation agreement with the U.S. and deep economic ties to the Gulf, the deal's outcome could reshape the security landscape of a region where millions of Indian nationals live and work.
